note: Ruled: belongs to Monitoring. Four of the five declared gaps are closed and the fifth is stated rather than hidden. The sharpest was the callback receipt: nothing recorded a gateway callback at all, so a callback that never arrived and one that arrived and was rejected were the same absent row, and a payment outage showed up only as orders that quietly stopped appearing. Receipts now distinguish four cases — succeeded, failed, arrived-and-acted-on-by-nothing, and never-arrived, which is the one with no row — because each has a different fix. Two stock-writing paths that disagree about whether a change is traceable drive current_stock and the movement ledger apart, and the trail then cannot say why the shelf moved. Closed with setStock(), which is absolute rather than a delta because that is what the box actually is — somebody counted the shelf and is typing what they found — and derives the delta under the row lock so the movement line is right even if another process adjusted the same product a moment earlier. A recount that found what was expected writes an audit line but no movement: inventing a zero movement would be a lie, and a silent no-op looks identical to a change that failed. The owner scope is carried into the lock, so a seller reaching another shop's product finds nothing rather than another shop's stock. backend: database/migrations/2026_09_20_000001_create_feature_flags_table.php; app/Services/Platform/FeatureFlags.php (enabled/bucket/save/delete); managed at Admin -> Settings -> Feature Flags (App\Http\Controllers\Admin\Settings\FeatureFlagController, routes admin.settings.feature-flags.*), listed in the settings index
note: Ruled: belongs in Admin, and it is built. There was no flag table, no config and no per-seller or per-percentage switch anywhere; the only lever was publishing or unpublishing an entire addon module, so every change to the marketplace went live for every seller and every shopper at the same moment and the only way back was a deployment. Three rules make the answer trustworthy, and each is held by a test because getting any of them wrong turns a safety mechanism into a source of incidents. A flag that does not exist is OFF — not an error and not on, because a rollout is opt-in and an unknown key is a typo or a removed flag. The same subject always gets the same answer: the bucket is a hash of the flag key and the subject, so a shop stays on the same side of the line across every request and device, where a random draw per request would show one seller two versions of the product in a single session. And the master switch beats the pilot list, which beats the percentage — an off switch some people are exempt from is not an off switch. The flag key is validated to the shape the code asks for, because a key that does not match is a control an operator reaches for during an incident that silently does nothing. An unreadable flag table means the old behaviour everywhere: a rollout that cannot be read must never fail open.
